Your Company’s Fraud Defenses Aren’t Ready for AI Threats

by Zacharia H. Baldwin

October 28, 2026
Deagreez/Getty Images
  • Post
  • Buy Copies

Summary.   

AI is making familiar voices, faces, and documents easy to counterfeit, allowing fraudsters to exploit gaps between business functions even when individual systems remain secure. To identify these vulnerabilities, leaders should trace high-risk...

Instaread

In the early 1960s, Tino De Angelis, a New Jersey commodities trader, secured loans with his warehouse receipts, claiming that his company, Allied Crude Vegetable Oil Refining, had vegetable oil stores in tanks in Bayonne. But most of that oil did not exist. Many tanks held seawater with just enough film of oil on top to fool an inspector checking from the hatch, and pipes between the tanks let Allied move the same oil into whichever tank was being tested. When the real receipts ran short, Allied forged more on a stolen American Express receipt book. When the scheme came apart in 1963, roughly $175 million in collateral turned out not to exist. The lenders never truly relied on just the oil. They relied on the name printed on every receipt, American Express Field Warehousing Corporation, and treated that trusted name as proof that someone had checked.

Sixty-one years later, a finance employee in the Hong Kong office of the British engineering firm Arup received an email from someone he believed was the company’s chief financial officer in the UK, detailing a confidential transaction. The email appeared legitimate in its form, but the employee was suspicious and did what his training told him to do: verify. The criminals were ready for that and arranged a video call. When the employee signed on, the CFO was on the call, along with colleagues the employee knew by sight and voice, and they told him to proceed. He trusted what he had seen and completed fifteen transfers, roughly HK$200 million (about US$25 million). However, every person on that call was AI-generated from publicly available videos of the colleagues.

The part of this scheme that should bother executives is not the deepfake. What should be concerning is that Arup said afterward that none of its internal systems had been compromised, and as far as anyone can tell, that is true. The email and the video platform worked, and so did the payment rails, which moved the money on valid instructions from a properly authenticated, duly authorized employee.

The cases share a similarity: Trust in a single piece of information. In the vegetable oil fraud, it was receipts; in the Arup case, it was convincing images and voices of trusted colleagues. That information acts as a point of trust. It can be official, like a warehouse receipt, or unofficial, like a familiar face on a video call. A point of trust is different from a point of failure. When a system fails, the process stops and someone notices it. When trusted information is false, nothing stops. The payment goes through, and no one notices until it’s too late; the money is gone.

The Arup case is not unique. In 2025 the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, run by colleagues of mine at the FBI, logged $20.9 billion in reported losses, $3.05 billion of it business email compromise.

Institutions keep locking down payment platforms, authenticating identities, monitoring transactions, and vetting vendors, and the work often pays off: Individual systems are much harder to compromise now. So, fraudsters go around them. Securing a system and securing a transaction are different jobs, and many institutions do only the first. The problem is that a control usually lives inside one function, but a payment does not.

Look at how most large payments move. They start as an email, become an approval, land in a payment platform, go out as a message to a correspondent bank, and end up as a line in the general ledger: six functions, four systems, two jurisdictions, one transaction. Each of those environments can be airtight, yet the crossings between them, the seams, are not.

Today’s financial fraudsters hunt for those seams the way a traditional cyber actor moves laterally through a network. For a criminal, the first system is rarely the objective; it is the route to the next one. The Arup approach seems to have been built on two facts about the company—that Hong Kong would act on instructions from London, and that the CFO’s face and voice were already on the internet. Neither fact alone is a vulnerability in any system, but together they were enough to execute the fraud.

Why Familiar Signals Are No Longer Reliable

One thing that changed between Bayonne and Hong Kong is the price of trust. De Angelis needed a tank farm and years of standing in the trade to build trust. The crew that hit Arup needed a video clip and AI software. That collapse matters because firms document the formal controls they designed but rely heavily on informal ones that evolved on their own.

For generations, employees leaned on known signals that quietly did the work of formal controls: a voice on the phone that sounded like Dave in accounting, a customer whose quarterly wire always landed the same week, an executive who never once wrote “kindly,” or an invoice that just looked off. Nobody tested any of those signals, and few auditors ever pulled a sample. Yet all of them were load-bearing.

Generative AI made every one of those signals cheap to counterfeit. A voice? Clone it from a panel discussion posted on YouTube. A writing style? Feed a model six emails. An invoice, a bank confirmation letter, the photo page of a passport, a face on a video call—generate it and move on. What these tools really counterfeit is the relationship behind the document or the voice: the years a supplier spent becoming familiar, the standing that made an executive’s word sufficient. The controls on paper look the same as last year; the assumptions under them have changed.

Map the Transaction, Not the Org Chart

Most large institutions already own more frameworks than they can use, and each new one adds seams of its own. What they may lack is a map. Boards ask good questions: Is the payment system secure? Is onboarding controlled? Every one of those usually stops at the edge of a system. Few boards ask what happens to a transaction as it crosses from one system into the next.

To begin addressing this problem, pick the three or four highest-value or highest-velocity flows in the business. Trace each one from origin to final accounting entry, across functions and legal entities, the way an examiner would. Then mark every transition where:

  • Information changes hands
  • Authority changes hands
  • Value changes form
  • Jurisdiction changes
  • Responsibility changes

Those are the seams: the places where a transaction is most exposed and least owned. At each seam, ask three questions:

  1. What is the receiving system assuming about what it just got?
  2. What evidence does it actually receive, as opposed to what everyone presumes it receives?
  3. Who verifies that evidence through a channel the sender does not control?

Most verification confirms that a document is well formed rather than whether the fact underneath it is true. Ask what happens when the evidence is false but perfectly formatted—is the answer nothing at all?

Question three is where the fix lives. The Arup employee checked the request through a video call the criminals had set up. The check that would have worked was a call he started himself, to a number from the company directory. Every check like that adds friction, and each company must decide how much risk it will accept in exchange for speed and ease of use. If every employee has to make that call for every transaction, people will start working around it. Many companies already use approval thresholds, requiring more signoffs as the dollar amount rises. The same logic applies here: Put the extra check on the handful of seams where money leaves and cannot be recalled, and it holds.

Name a person for each seam in those priority flows, with a written answer to the three questions and the authority to stop a payment that can’t be verified. That person should never be the one who requests, approves, or processes the payment. When the same employee can both make a payment happen and confirm it, there is no independent check. Investigators see that gap constantly in small business embezzlement. AI makes it worse. An insider can now create a convincing invoice or email to support fake payments as easily as an outside criminal can fake a CFO. In a small company, the right person might be the owner or an outside trusted accountant. In a large one, it should be someone senior enough to see the whole process. Either way, find out how long it actually takes to stop payments before the day you need to. That small point of friction almost never exists where the fraud thrives.

. . .

In many cases, better technology genuinely helps prevent cyberfraud: detection improves, and authentication gets harder to spoof. But if the weakness is that two systems trust each other without checking what crosses between them, a sharper tool inside either one leaves the seam where it was.

Companies have become very good at defending what they own. The next decade of fraud risk will turn on how well they defend what sits in between. An org chart shows who owns which system. The transaction shows where the risk travels, and that is the map criminals are working from when they try to take advantage of companies’ weaknesses.

Zacharia H. Baldwin is a supervisory special agent at the FBI, where he is program coordinator for the Financial Crimes and Illicit Finance threat in the Miami Division and oversees a Complex Financial Crimes squad. He previously served in the Money Laundering, Forfeiture, and Bank Fraud Unit at FBI Headquarters as program manager for the Virtual Currency and Business Email Compromise sub-threats. He is an FBI-designated subject matter expert in Financial Crimes and Money Laundering and a Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent the position of the Federal Bureau of Investigation or the U.S. Department of Justice.
